# Summary and questions
This this section we review that at which time a POVM can be simulated by a projective measurement.


# Projective Simulations of Quantum Measurements
Projective measurement $\mathbb{P}(d,n)$ are n-outcome POVMs on d-dimensional Hilbert space whose effects are orthogonal projectors.
We denote $\mathbb{SP}(d,n)$ as n-outcome POVMs on d-dimensional Hilbert space that can be simulated by classical post-processing projective measurements.
In other words, $\mathbb{SP}(d,n)$ is the convex hull of the POVMs sets $\mathbb{P}(d,n)$:
$$
\begin{align}
\mathbb{P}(d,n):\{\{M_1,\cdots,M_n\}| M_j \succeq 0, \sum_{j} M_j = \mathbb{I}(d), M_jM_k = M_j \delta_{jk}\} .
\mathbb{SP}(d,n): \mathrm{Conv}[\mathbb{P}(d,n)]
\end{align}
$$

A way to quanttify the closeness of a POVM $\mathbf{M}$ is to check whether its mixing with idnetity could became a PVM:
$$
t(\mathbf{M}) = \max\{ t | \Phi_t(\mathbf{M}):= tM_i + (1-t)\frac{\mathrm{tr}(M_i)\mathbb{I}}{d} \in \mathbb{SP}(d, n)\}
$$
